outcome: No new edge proposed. Leopold is a precursor, not a historian; his documented relationships with historians in the atlas are to Cronon and Worster, both already edges. New readings strengthen those two edges and are offered as source addenda. Other leads rest on interviewer remarks, a single non-endpoint reader, or unread texts.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Already represented by edge_1245. New corroboration (source addenda): Cronon's History 901 syllabus, Fall 1994 (archived copy of the University of Wisconsin PDF, read 2026-10-31) lists A Sand County Almanac among the seminar's bookstore texts (PDF p. 2), assigns 'Good Oak' (pp. 6–19) in 'Reading the Landscape, Part I' on 28 September alongside Watts's Reading the Landscape of America and a postglacial vegetation history (PDF p. 4), and assigns 'Thinking Like a Mountain' and Part IV, 'The Upshot', in 'A Special Affection for Things Wild' on 16 November (PDF p. 6).

Already represented by edge_1251. New corroboration: in The Wealth of Nature (OUP, 1993), 'Restoring a Natural Order' opens on Worster's visit to the Wisconsin land Leopold bought in 1935 (chapter opening read 2026-10-31 in the Crossref/OUP abstract, doi:10.1093/oso/9780195092646.003.0017); chapter body unread.

Not proposed. In Merchant's 2022 Bancroft oral history (project copy of the Berkeley PDF, searched 2026-10-31) Leopold is mentioned only by the interviewer (PDF leaf 31, a question about Muir and Leopold in Wisconsin); Merchant's answer turns to Hugh Iltis. No Merchant text on Leopold's land ethic (e.g. Radical Ecology, 1992) could be read lawfully.

Not proposed. Graeme Wynn (Acadiensis 31:1, 2001; UNB journal PDF re-read 2026-10-31) titles his essay as a gesture to Leopold (p. 129), uses 'Good Oak' as an allegory for historical-geographical method (pp. 142–143, n. 48) and writes that 'few are better situated than historical geographers to respond to Leopold's call' (p. 145) — and adds 'Few have done so'; and Wynn is not an atlas endpoint. One programmatic reading is not evidence of uptake by the field; MacEachern (2002, p. 219) warns against assuming Canadians read Leopold. Leopold already sits on the geography roster without an edge; a reviewer may wish to decide whether a roster edge is wanted.

Searched without a verified omission. McNeill 2003 (History and Theory) was read earlier at pp. 8, 14–16 without a Leopold passage; White's 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay and the 1990 JAH round-table responses (Crosby, White) are paywalled and unread for Leopold.

source_addenda.cronon_environment_syllabus_1994: Addendum 2026-10-31 (thin-person-edges, Leopold and Carson): the live URL now returns 404; read in the Internet Archive Wayback capture of 25 July 2024 (web.archive.org/web/20240725060840/…history901_fall1994_cronon.pdf), 6 pp. PDF p. 1: 'History 901 … Topics in American Environmental History', instructor Bill Cronon, Fall 1994, a seminar reading recent environmental history 'principally for the theories and methodologies it can offer scholars'. PDF p. 2: bookstore texts include Carson, Silent Spring, and Leopold, Sand County Almanac. PDF p. 4: 28 September, 'Reading the Landscape, Part I': Leopold, 'Good Oak', 6–19. PDF p. 6: 16 November, 'A Special Affection for Things Wild': Leopold, 137–41, 237–95 ('Thinking Like a Mountain' and 'The Upshot'); 30 November, 'Toxic Politics': Carson, Silent Spring, 1–37, 103–27, 187–98.
source_addenda.p4c_worster_wealth_oup: Addendum 2026-10-31 (thin-person-edges, Leopold): the OUP chapter openings in Crossref also show 'Restoring a Natural Order' (doi:10.1093/oso/9780195092646.003.0017) opening on Worster's visit to Wisconsin, 'looking for a place where a man had given his life': the land bought in 1935 by Aldo Leopold, who planted it for thirteen years. Opening paragraph only.
